Line up per-species modules across species

Source: R/joint_modules.R
joint_modules.Rd

Lines up the modules of each species into shared labels. The same label in two species is the same module. Modules come from detect_modules(), one species at a time.

Usage

joint_modules(nets, orthologs, modules = NULL, lambda = 1, seed = NULL)

Arguments

nets

Named list of at least two compute_network() results, dense or sparse. The names are the species.

orthologs

Long table with columns species, gene, hog, or a file for read_orthologs().

modules

Named list with one detect_modules() or as_modules() result per species of nets, in any order. Each must label every gene of its network. NULL runs detect_modules() on each species.

lambda

Weight of the hog term against the co-expression term. One number of 0 or more. At 0 no label spans two species.

seed

Integer seed, or NULL to use the current stream.

Value

A list with:

modules

Named list with one module assignment per species, in the order of nets. Each has the as_modules() shape: modules (named integer vector, gene -> shared label), module_genes, n_modules, method = "joint" and params.

members

Data frame with one row per species module: species, module (the label in modules), label (the shared label) and n_genes. Rows are sorted by label, species in nets order, then module.

hogs

Data frame with one row per hog with two or more copies among the network genes, sorted by hog: hog, n_copies, n_modules (distinct shared labels among the copies), module_main (the label with most copies; a tie goes to the smallest label) and copies_main (copies in it).

params

List of lambda, gamma (1), seed, modules_given and quality (the objective of the final labels).

Details

Each module of each species is one node. Louvain joins these nodes into shared labels. It never moves a single gene, so labels are species modules lined up, never genes clustered again. A shared label may hold several modules of one species. It may hold modules of one species only, when nothing lines up.

The objective has two terms. Within a species, it is modularity with that species' own null. Across species, it is the hog overlap of two modules against the overlap expected for that species pair. A hog with c_s copies in species s and c_t in species t gives each copy pair the weight 1 / (c_s c_t). So hogs with many copies count less. The edges are those at or above each species' threshold. Each species' edge weights are divided by its largest weight.

On wood and leaf, every lambda from 0.25 to 16 gave the same labels. For why family-steered clustering of genes was withdrawn, see dev/design-notes/hypergraph-community-literature.md, sections 10-12.

See also

detect_modules() for one species, module_correspondence() for pairs of species with p-values, module_preservation() to test a module in another species.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
res <- joint_modules(list(A = net_a, B = net_b), "orthologs.tsv",
  seed = 1
)
res$members
res$hogs[res$hogs$n_modules > 1, ]
} # }
